title: Reading a generative-AI paper in 20 minutes

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the primary goal of reading a generative AI paper in 20 minutes?
options: To memorize every equation and detail in the appendix
To develop spatial intuition to judge if a model is a solid structure or a mirage
To download and fine-tune the model immediately
To verify the standard deviations of all reported metrics
questions.answer: To develop spatial intuition to judge if a model is a solid structure or a mirage
questions.why: The lesson states: 'Your goal in this 400-level course is not to memorize every equation, but to develop the spatial intuition to judge whether a new model is a solid structure or a mirage.'

questions.q: In the 'cake' analogy for reading a paper, what do the middle layers represent?
questions.why: The lesson states: 'The middle layers are the Method and Results, which show you the recipe and the taste test.'

questions.q: What is the formula for calculating Relative Improvement ($\Delta$) as defined in the lesson?
questions.why: The lesson explicitly defines the formula as: '$\Delta = (R - B) / B$' where R is the reported metric and B is the baseline metric.

questions.q: Based on the lab results, why did Model C's claim not survive scrutiny?
options: The improvement was negative, indicating a performance drop
The relative improvement was approximately 0.7%, which is below the 2% noise threshold
The baseline metric was too weak to be a valid comparison
The paper did not report standard deviations for the F1 score
questions.answer: The relative improvement was approximately 0.7%, which is below the 2% noise threshold
questions.why: The lab output for Model C shows a relative improvement of 0.00699308 (approx 0.7%). The lesson states: 'This is well below the 2% threshold. Therefore, this claim does not survive; it is likely within the noise of the measurement.'

questions.q: According to the 'Common mistakes' section, why is comparing a new model to a weak baseline problematic?
questions.answer: It makes the improvement look larger than it is.
questions.why: The lesson lists 'Ignoring the Baseline' as a common mistake and explains: 'Comparing a new model to a weak baseline makes the improvement look larger than it is.'
